title: Pack the bag: one array, filled left to right
limits: n ≤ 6, W ≤ 30, every weight ≤ 30, every worth ≤ 100
why: Going through the capacities upwards, best[c − w] may already include the item being processed, so the same item is taken twice or more. Each item may be used once: the capacities must be walked downwards, so that best[c − w] is still the value from before this item.
nudges: When best[c] is updated from best[c − w], which items has best[c − w] already been allowed to use?
What does the program print for a single light, valuable item and a large W?

title: Museum: sweep over arrivals and departures
why: At a shared minute the program handles the departure before the arrival, because sorting pairs puts (minute, −1) before (minute, +1). But both ends of a visit are included: someone leaving at minute 3 and someone arriving at minute 3 are inside together during minute 3, and the program never sees them together.
nudges: In what order does sort put two events that share the same minute?
One visitor leaves at minute 3 and another arrives at minute 3. Are they ever inside together?

title: Walls: the first time a cell is reached
why: A plain queue reaches each cell by a route with the fewest steps, and the program keeps whatever number of walls that first route happened to break. A longer way round through free cells can break fewer walls. Steps onto free cells cost 0 and steps onto walls cost 1, so free steps must be handled before wall steps (a two-ended queue), not in order of arrival.
nudges: In what order does a plain queue reach the cells: by walls broken, or by something else?
Can a route with more steps break fewer walls than every route with the fewest steps?

title: Job order: heaviest first
limits: n ≤ 6, every time and every weight between 1 and 20
why: Weight alone ignores how long a job keeps every later job waiting. A slightly heavier job that takes very long delays everything after it, and that delay can cost far more than going first saves.
nudges: If two jobs stand next to each other in the order and you swap them, which costs change?
How long would a job have to be before a slightly lighter, very short job should go ahead of it?

title: Cables: from each town, the cheapest cable onwards
limits: n ≤ 6, m ≤ 10, every cost between 1 and 20, no pair of towns listed twice
why: The program only looks at cables leaving the town it joined last. A cheapest network may branch, so it misses cheaper cables that leave towns joined earlier, and it gives up at a dead end while other towns are still waiting.
nudges: Does a cheapest network have to be one long line of towns?
What does the program print when its walk reaches a town with no cable to anywhere new, but other towns are still not joined?

title: Jobs: everyone takes the cheapest job left
why: The first person takes their cheapest job without asking what that costs the others. If that job is the only cheap one for somebody later, the small saving now is paid back many times over.
nudges: Who pays for the choice the first person makes?
Can you make a job that is slightly the cheapest for person 1 and enormously the cheapest for person 2?

title: Pack the bag: best worth per weight first
limits: n ≤ 6, W ≤ 30, every weight ≤ 30, every worth ≤ 100
why: Worth per weight is the right order only if items could be cut. An item that is taken whole can leave room that nothing else fills, and then two slightly worse items that fill the bag exactly beat it.
nudges: What would this program do if the items could be cut into pieces?
After the first item is taken, how much room can be left that no other item fits into?

title: Piles: always merge the lightest neighbouring pair
why: The cheapest merge now can glue together two piles that belonged in different halves of the best plan. Every stone is paid for once per merge it takes part in, and a cheap merge in the middle makes the middle stones take part in more merges than they need to.
nudges: How many times is each stone paid for in the sample, under the best plan?
If the two middle piles are merged first, how many more merges do their stones still go through?

title: Two baskets: each apple into the lighter basket
why: Putting each apple into the lighter basket keeps the baskets close at every moment, but the best split may need them far apart for a while: the two heaviest apples sometimes belong together, balanced by all the small ones. The program can never put its two heaviest apples into the same basket.
nudges: Where do the two heaviest apples always end up under this rule?
Can you choose weights where the two heaviest apples together equal all the others together?

title: Increasing numbers: take every number that fits
why: Keeping a number just because it fits can be a mistake: a large number kept early blocks several smaller ones that come later. Which numbers to skip is a real choice, and the program never skips one that fits.
nudges: Once the program keeps a number, can it ever change its mind about it?
What happens when a very large number stands right after the starting position?

title: Two trades: the best single trade first
why: The best pair of trades need not contain the best single trade. When the price dips in the middle of the best single trade, selling before the dip and buying again in it earns more than holding through, and the program never splits its first trade.
nudges: Must the best single trade be one of the two trades in the best pair?
What does a dip in the middle of a long rise offer to someone allowed two trades?

title: Chosen vertices: the larger colour class
why: A colour class is one valid choice, but the best choice may mix the two colours: vertices of different colours can be chosen together whenever no edge joins them. Leaves hanging from two neighbouring centres have different colours, yet all of them can be chosen at once.
nudges: Two vertices of different colours: are they always joined by an edge?
Which vertices would you certainly want to choose in a tree with many leaves?

title: Longest route: the two deepest branches below vertex 1
why: The longest route does not have to pass through vertex 1. When both of its ends lie inside one branch below vertex 1, the program never measures it.
nudges: Does the longest route in a tree have to pass through vertex 1?
Where could two long branches meet, other than at vertex 1?

title: Calm stretch: start again when the budget breaks
limits: n ≤ 8, S ≤ 30, every number between 1 and 20
why: When the budget breaks, the program throws the whole stretch away and starts again at the current number. The best stretch can begin in the middle of the stretch that was just abandoned, and the program never looks there.
nudges: When a number does not fit, how much of the current stretch really has to be given up?
Could the best stretch begin inside a stretch the program has already thrown away?
